slides.title: Homogeneous Model
slides.notes: Open by naming the chapter's modeling bargain: add one coordinate so locations, directions, offset flats, and projective maps can be handled by linear algebra in a larger space. Emphasize that this is not a new physical axis. It is a representation device that makes incidence programmable.

slides.title: Representation Space
slides.notes: Use the scale-ray picture to separate a homogeneous representative from the finite point it names. Any nonzero scalar multiple lies on the same representation ray, and the affine chart reads the point only after dividing by weight. This is why raw coordinate length is not geometric evidence.

slides.title: Finite And Infinite Points
slides.notes: Slow down at the zero-weight line. Students often hear point at infinity as a poetic phrase; here it is a precise direction carrier. Finite points have recoverable locations, while zero-weight representatives store attitudes. Parallelism becomes an incidence event instead of an exception branch.

slides.title: Weights And Addition
slides.notes: Frame addition as a contract rather than a universal geometric operation. If the weights represent masses or barycentric coefficients, normalizing a sum has meaning. If the scales are arbitrary, the same array addition may be meaningless. The difference of equal-weight finite points is the clean direction example.

slides.title: Lines As Joins
slides.notes: Present the line as the span of two homogeneous point vectors. In coordinates the dual line equation is familiar, but the construction is more general: join creates a flat, and the incidence test asks whether another point belongs to that span or satisfies the corresponding equation.

slides.title: Parallel Lines Meet
slides.notes: This slide is the first major payoff. Two nonparallel lines meet at a finite point, while parallel lines meet at a zero-weight point recording their shared direction. The operation does not fail; the interpretation changes according to the weight of the returned representative.

slides.title: Flats As Blades
slides.notes: Move from lines to the general rule. A k-dimensional offset flat in the base space is represented directly by a k plus one blade in the homogeneous space. The extra spanning factor carries location information, while the other factors carry attitude. That grade shift is the organizing memory hook.

slides.title: Direct And Dual
slides.notes: Keep the two representations conceptually distinct. Direct blades are built from spanning points and directions; dual flats are equations that annihilate incident points. Both describe the same geometry, but they transform differently. This distinction prevents a common implementation bug when moving lines and planes.

slides.title: Incidence Engine
slides.notes: Now assemble the workflow. Joins build containing flats, meets recover common subflats, and residual tests confirm incidence. In three dimensions this includes line-plane meetings and Plucker-style line diagnostics. The main teaching point is generic data flow: fewer special cases, more algebraic classification.

slides.title: Affine Versus Projective
slides.notes: Contrast the last row of the matrix. Affine maps keep the line at infinity fixed, so parallelism is preserved. A projective map can move that line, so formerly parallel finite lines can acquire a finite vanishing point. Incidence remains trustworthy even when metric intuition changes.

slides.title: Cross Ratio
slides.notes: Use cross ratio as the chapter's positive invariant story. The apparent spacing of four collinear points may change dramatically under a projective transformation, but the projective ratio survives. This is a useful measurement when a camera image has incidence but lacks an honest Euclidean ruler.

slides.title: Conics And Projection
slides.notes: Explain conics as a boundary case for the blade language. Lines and planes are flats, but conics are quadratic incidence equations. They still fit homogeneous transformation rules, and perspective projection can be read as repeatedly joining a camera center to a point and meeting an image plane.

slides.title: Model Limits
slides.notes: Make the warning explicit before students overuse the model. Homogeneous coordinates are excellent for incidence, affine maps, projective maps, and ratios, but a naive representation-space inner product is not Euclidean distance. Metric questions must be dehomogenized or handed to a richer model.

slides.title: Carry Forward
slides.notes: Close with a model-selection checklist. Use homogeneous algebra when the problem is about points, flats, incidence, projection, and projective transformations. Reach for the vector-space model for pure directions and rotors, and later reach for conformal tools when distances, spheres, and Euclidean motions must be native.
